answers: The new name of the income tax law for 2025 is the **Income-tax Act, 2025**. This is stated in Section 1(1) of the Act.

The Income-tax Act 2025 shall come into force on the 1st April, 2026. This is stated in Section 3 of the Act, which specifies that it shall be deemed to have come into force on that date. 

Source: Section 3 of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you earn money from a business outside India and are not ordinarily resident in India, your income from that business may be deemed to accrue or arise in India, depending on the circumstances. This is governed by **Section 9(1)(i)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that:

> "Transaction in respect of any goods, services or property carried out by such non-resident with any person in India, including provision of download of data or software in India, if the aggregate of payments arising from such transaction or transactions during the tax year exceeds such amount as may be prescribed."

This provision applies if the business is conducted in India, or if the aggregate payments exceed the prescribed amount. 

However, if the business is entirely outside India and does not involve transactions in India, the income may not be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The determination depends on whether the business is connected to India through a "business connection" as defined in **Section 9(1)(a)**, which includes activities carried out in India or through a person who has an authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the non-resident. 

For a precise determination, the relevant provisions of the Income-Tax Act 2025 must be consulted.

The income received in India through a balance sheet prepared in India is considered as income received in India for tax purposes. This is based on Section 5(3) of the Income Tax Act 2025, which states that income accruing or arising outside India shall not be deemed to be received in India under this section by reason only of the fact that it is taken into account in a balance sheet prepared in India. 

Source: Section 5(3) of the Income Tax Act 2025.

If you are a citizen of India and visit India for a short period, you may still be considered a resident in India for tax purposes, depending on the duration of your stay. 

According to **Section 6(2)(b)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, an individual is deemed to be resident in India if they are in India cumulatively for **sixty days or more** during the tax year and have been in India cumulatively for **three hundred and sixty-five days or more** in the four years preceding the tax year. However, **Section 6(5)** states that if your total income exceeds fifteen lakh rupees during the tax year (other than income from foreign sources), sub-section (2)(b) applies as if the word "sixty days" had been substituted with "one hundred and twenty days".

If you are a citizen of India and visit India for a short period, you may still be deemed a resident if you meet the criteria of **Section 6(2)(b)** or **Section 6(5)**. However, if your stay is short and you do not meet the cumulative days requirement, you may not be deemed a resident. 

For precise determination, you should consult a tax professional or refer to the specific provisions of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If your total income from sources in India exceeds fifteen lakh rupees, you may be considered a resident in India under Section 6(7) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, provided you meet the other criteria for being deemed a resident. However, this does not automatically mean you are a resident if you are not physically present for a long time. The determination of residency is based on cumulative days spent in India and other factors specified in the Act. 

Source: Section 6(7) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Dividend income is deemed to be received in the tax year in which it is declared, distributed, or paid, as specified in Section 7(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. Additionally, interim dividends are deemed to be received in the tax year in which they are unconditionally made available to the member, as per Section 7(2)(b). 

Source: Section 7(2)(a) and (b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, an interim dividend is taxed in the tax year in which the amount of such dividend is unconditionally made available by the company to the member who is entitled to it. This is specified in Section 7(2)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If a husband and wife are governed by the community of property system in Goa or Daman and Diu, their income shall not be assessed together as that of such community of property. This is specified in **Section 10(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Under the community of property system in Goa and the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, the salary income of a spouse is included in the total income of the spouse who has actually earned it. This is specified in **Section 10(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

If one spouse earns salary and the other does not, the salary income is taxed separately in the hands of the spouse who earned it. The other spouse's income (excluding salary) is divided equally between them, as per **Section 10(b)**. 

Thus, the salary income is taxed separately in the hands of the spouse who earned it, and the other spouse's income is treated as divided equally. 

**Source:** Section 10(a) and Section 10(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

According to Section 11 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, incomes enumerated in Schedules II, III, IV, V, and VI are not included in total income, subject to fulfillment of conditions specified in those schedules. Therefore, income from specific sources (as outlined in the schedules and exceptions) may be excluded from total taxable income.

If a political party or electoral trust does not meet the conditions mentioned in Schedule VIII, the income enumerated in Schedule VIII shall be charged to tax under this Act for that tax year. This is specified in Section 12(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, salary includes payments made for unused leave. According to Section 16( h) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, "salary" includes any payment received by an employee in respect of any period of leave not availed of by him. The source for this is Section 16( h) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

According to Section 16 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, "annual accretion" to the balance at the credit of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent to which it is chargeable to tax as per paragraph 6 of Part A of Schedule XI, is included in "salary". 

Source: Section 16 of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you receive rent for a property that was due in the past but you only receive it this year, the treatment for tax purposes depends on whether the rent is considered "unrealised rent" as defined in **Section 23** of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

- **Section 23(1)** states that the amount of arrears of rent received by an assessee from a tenant, or the unrealised rent realised subsequently from a tenant, shall be deemed to be income from house property in respect of the tax year in which such rent is received or realised.  
- **Section 23(2)** further states that this deemed income is included in the total income of the assessee under the head "Income from house property," regardless of whether the assessee is the owner of the property or not.  
- **Section 23(3)** allows a deduction of 30% of the arrears of rent or the unrealised rent, as specified in the section.

Thus, the rent received this year for a property that was due in the past is treated as income from house property for the current tax year, and a deduction of 30% of this amount may be allowed.  

Source: **Section 23** of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, you can claim a deduction of 30% on arrears of rent or unrealised rent received subsequently, as per Section 23 of the Income-Tax Act 2025. This provision states that the amount of arrears of rent or unrealised rent received subsequently shall be deemed to be income from house property, and 30% of such amount is allowed as deduction. 

Source: Section 23(3) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The income from rent, rates, taxes, repairs, and insurance in a business or profession is calculated as follows:

1. **Rent**: The rent paid by the assessee when the premises are occupied as a tenant is allowed as a deduction under Section 28(1)(c).  
   - **Source**: Section 28(1)(c) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

2. **Rates, Taxes, and Land Revenue**: These are allowed as deductions under Section 28(1)(b).  
   - **Source**: Section 28(1)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

3. **Repairs and Insurance**:  
   - **Current repairs (not capital expenditure)**: Allowed as deductions under Section 28(1)(d) and (e).  
   - **Insurance premium**: Allowed as a deduction under Section 28(1)(a).  
   - **Repairs to machinery, plant, or furniture**: Allowed as deductions under Section 28(1)(f).  
   - **Source**: Section 28(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

4. **Restrictions on Deductions**: If the premises, machinery, plant, or furniture is partly used for the business or profession, the deduction allowable under Section 28(1) is restricted to the fair proportionate part thereof as determined by the Assessing Officer.  
   - **Source**: Section 28(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

This calculation is part of the computation of profits and gains of business or profession under Section 27.  
- **Source**: Section 27 of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, there are exceptions when calculating profits from a business or profession related to rent, rates, taxes, repairs, and insurance. According to Section 28 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, the following amounts are allowed as deductions:

- Any premium paid in respect of insurance against risk of damage or destruction thereof (Section 28(a)).
- Land revenue, local rates or municipal taxes paid (Section 28(b)).
- Rent paid, when the premises are occupied by the assessee as a tenant (Section 28(c)).
- Amount paid on account of current repairs to the premises, not being in the nature of capital expenditure, when the premises are occupied by the assessee otherwise than as a tenant (Section 28(d)).
- Amount paid on account of cost of repairs, not being in the nature of capital expenditure, when the premises are occupied by the assessee as a tenant and where he has undertaken to bear the cost of repairs to the premises (Section 28(e)).
- The amount paid on account of current repairs to machinery, plant or furniture, not being in the nature of capital expenditure (Section 28(f)).

Additionally, if the premises, building, machinery, plant or furniture is partly used or not wholly and exclusively used for the purposes of the business or profession, the deduction allowable under sub-section (1) shall be restricted to the fair proportionate part thereof as determined by the Assessing Officer (Section 28(2)).

There are also exceptions under Section 38 and Section 55, which relate to certain sums deemed as profits and gains of business or profession, and profits from insurance business, respectively.

Yes, you can claim a deduction for expenses like market surveys or feasibility reports when starting a new business in India, provided the expenses are incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession. 

This is governed by **Section 34** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that any expenditure (not being an expenditure of the nature specified in sections 28 to 33, 44 to 49, 51 and 52, or not being capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession."

Therefore, expenses such as market surveys or feasibility reports are generally deductible under **Section 34**.

- The expenditure is **not the cost of any land or building**.  
- The project is **notified by the Board** as per the guidelines issued by it.

If you claim a deduction for a skill development project, you may not claim it under any other tax rule for the same year, provided the conditions of **Section 47** are met. Specifically, the expenditure on a skill development project by a company is allowed as a deduction under **Section 47** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, provided the project is notified by the Board as per the guidelines issued by it. 

This means that the deduction under **Section 47** is **exclusive** for that year and cannot be claimed under any other provision of the Act for the same or any other tax year. 

**Source:** Section 47 (Expenditure on agricultural extension project and skill development project) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The deduction is allowed on the basis of deposits into the special account or deposit account, as specified in the Schedule IX. The amount of deduction is determined as per the provisions of the Schedule IX, and any amount withdrawn or utilized from the account at the time of closure or otherwise shall be charged to tax as per the provisions of the Schedule IX. 

Source: Section 48(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you sell an asset you bought under a government scheme for tea, coffee, or rubber production, the income from the sale may be exempt from tax under certain conditions. Specifically, if the asset was acquired under a government scheme (as defined in Section 536 of the Income-Tax Act 2025), and the sale is pursuant to an agreement or arrangement entered into by the Central Government or approved by it, the income may be exempt from tax. This is outlined in Section 536(11)(a) and (b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

The exemption is subject to the conditions that the agreement or arrangement is notified by the Central Government with regard to the national interest, and the foreign company (or relevant entity) is not engaged in any activity in India other than the one resulting in the income. 

If the asset is sold under these conditions, the income may not be included in your total income. However, if the sale does not meet these conditions, the income may be subject to tax.

Source: **Section 49(1)**, Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you sell an asset acquired under a government special scheme, the sale may be taxed in the year of the sale, depending on the specific provisions of the Income-Tax Act 2025. According to Section 536(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, if an asset is acquired as per the special scheme or deposit scheme and sold or transferred to any person before the expiry of eight years from the end of the tax year in which it was acquired, the part of the cost of the asset relating to the deduction allowed under paragraph 1 shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of business of the tax year in which such asset is sold or transferred and shall accordingly be charged to income-tax for that tax year. 

Therefore, the sale of such an asset may be taxed in the year of the sale.

This is applicable in certain cases where the consideration is less than the stamp duty value, and the provisions of Section 53(1) or (2) apply. The stamp duty value is deemed to be the full value of consideration for calculating profits and gains from transfer, subject to specific conditions. 

Source: Section 53(1) and (2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Therefore, if the stamp duty value is under 110% of the consideration received, the amount received can be considered as the full value for tax purposes. 

Source: Section 78(1)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Interest income from bad or doubtful debts of a scheduled bank is considered taxable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" in the tax year in which such interest is credited to the profit and loss account or actually received, whichever is earlier. This is specified in **Section 56(1)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The question of whether a co-operative bank falls under the special tax rule for interest on bad debts is addressed in **Section 56(1)(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

According to this section, **interest income on bad or doubtful debts of a specified financial institution** is chargeable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" in the tax year in which such interest is credited to the profit and loss account or actually received, whichever is earlier. 

A **specified financial institution** includes co-operative banks, as defined in **Section 56(1)(a)(ii)**. Therefore, **co-operative banks fall under the special tax rule for interest on bad debts**.

Source: **Section 56(1)(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

When a service contract lasts less than 90 days, the profit is calculated using the **project completion method** under Section 57(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. This method involves recognizing revenue and expenses based on the progress of the project.

According to Section 60 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, head office expenditure incurred outside India for business or professional purposes is allowable for deduction under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession," subject to the provisions of sub-section (1). 

The deduction is restricted to an upper monetary limit of 5% of the adjusted total income of the assessee, as specified in sub-section (2). 

Source: Section 60 of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The maximum limit for deducting head office expenses for a non-resident if their total income is a loss is **5% of the adjusted total income** of the non-resident, as specified in Section 60(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

Source: Section 60(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The section states that any person carrying on a specified profession or a business shall keep and maintain such books of account to enable the Assessing Officer to compute their total income under the Act. 

Source: Section 62(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you are a doctor or lawyer, you are considered to be in a specified profession under Section 62(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. Therefore, you are required to keep and maintain books of account as per the provisions of Section 62. This requirement applies regardless of your income level, including if your income is below the specified limits. 

Source: Section 62(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

According to Section 63(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, a person carrying on business or profession who meets the conditions specified in column B of the table shall get their accounts audited by an accountant before the specified date. If your business turnover exceeds one crore rupees, you are required to get your accounts audited. 

Even if most of your payments and receipts are made by cheque or bank draft, the requirement to get your accounts audited remains. Section 63(5)(a) states that the "specified date" for filing the audit report is one month prior to the due date for filing the income return under Section 263(1). The payment or receipt by cheque or bank draft is deemed to be in cash for the purpose of computing the audit. 

Therefore, you still need to get your books audited.

If your profession income exceeds fifty lakh rupees in any tax year, you are required to get your accounts audited under Section 63(1)(c) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. This requirement applies regardless of whether you have cash transactions. The audit is mandated by the law, and the presence of cash transactions does not exempt you from this obligation. 

Source: Section 63(1)(c) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Source: Section 70 of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

2. Such transfer does not attract tax on capital gains in the country in which the amalgamating company is incorporated.

This provision ensures that the transfer is not treated as a capital gain transaction in the foreign country, thereby avoiding capital gains tax.

- **C** = net asset value of the total portfolio immediately before segregation of portfolios.  

This is specified in **Section 73(1)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Source: Section 90(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, you can claim a deduction for commission paid to a banker to collect interest on your securities, provided the commission is allowed as a deduction under the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

According to **Section 32(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, **bonus or commission paid to an employee for services rendered** is allowed as a deduction if the amount would not have been payable as profits or dividend if it had not been paid as bonus or commission. 

For interest income on securities, **Section 153** of the Income-Tax Act 2025 allows a deduction for interest on deposits with banking companies, co-operative societies engaged in banking, or post offices, provided the interest is not on time deposits. 

However, **Section 393** of the Income-Tax Act 2025 specifies that interest income on securities is deductible at a rate of 10% if the threshold limit is met. 

The threshold limit for interest income on securities is **`10,000** for individuals and **`50,000** for persons other than senior citizens. 

Therefore, if the commission paid to the banker is for services rendered and falls within the scope of Section 32(a), it can be claimed as a deduction. If the commission is for collecting interest on securities, it may be deductible under Section 153, depending on the nature of the deposit and the applicable conditions. 

For precise details, refer to the relevant sections of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you cannot explain where your expenses came from, the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be income of the assessee for the tax year. This is specified in **Section 105(1)(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

This deemed income is not allowed as a deduction under the Act, as stated in **Section 105(2)**.

If an expense is incurred by the assessee and the assessee offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation is not satisfactory in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee for that tax year. This means that such expenditure may not be allowed as a deduction under the Income-Tax Act 2025. 

Source: Section 105(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, if you borrow money through a hundi or a cheque that is not payable to a specific account holder, the amount borrowed or repaid (including interest) shall be deemed to be the income of the person borrowing or repaying, as the case may be, for the tax year in which the amount was borrowed or repaid.  

**Source:** Section 106(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

According to Section 106 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, if an amount borrowed or repaid through a negotiable instrument or on a hundi is deemed to be the income of a person for the tax year in which the amount was borrowed or repaid, then the person shall not be liable to be assessed again in respect of such amount upon repayment. 

Source: Section 106(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

According to Section 111(1)(i) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, a loss from a short-term capital asset may be set off only against the income under the head "Capital gains" if any, assessable for that tax year in respect of any other capital asset.
